Radar absorbing structures (RAS) can bear load and absorb electromagnetic waves to reduce radar cross section (RCS).
The composites studied consist of glass fibers, carbon fibers, epoxy resin, and carbon nanotubes (CNTs).
Permittivity measurements were performed using a HP8510B network analyzer in the 8.2–12.4 GHz frequency range.
Increasing CNT content in the composites increases both the real and imaginary parts of permittivity.
Specimens were prepared by dispersing CNTs ultrasonically in epoxy resin and curing under 6 atm pressure.
Specimens were cut to 22.86 x 10.16 mm² to fit rectangular waveguides for permittivity measurement.
Air gaps between specimen and waveguide were sealed with silver paste to reduce measurement error.
A genetic algorithm (GA) was used to optimize triple-layer RAS designs for minimal reflection loss.
The maximum total thickness for simulated RAS was limited to 5.0 mm.
The optimal triple-layer RAS design had a peak reflection loss of -43.52 dB and a -10 dB absorption bandwidth of 3.19 GHz.
Reflection loss below -20 dB corresponds to 99% absorption of incident electromagnetic power.
The GA optimization linked reflection loss analysis with layer thickness and CNT content variables.
The back surface of the RAS was assumed to be a perfect conductor in simulations.
The six optimized triple-layer RAS cases showed varying absorption bandwidths from 2.60 GHz to 3.19 GHz.
Fiber reinforced polymeric composites allow tailoring of electromagnetic properties by adjusting composition and stacking sequences.
The complex permittivity is expressed as εr = εr' - jεr'', where εr' is the real part and εr'' is the imaginary part.
The complex permeability µr also affects microwave absorption but was not the main focus in this study.
The study confirms that CNT-filled composites can be effectively designed as radar absorbing structures.
The reflection loss was calculated using an objective function integrating reflection coefficient squared over frequency.
The study used a planar rectangular mold for specimen preparation and curing at room temperature for about 2 hours.
